updates.summary: Binding rules (35 articles) for providers using algorithmic recommendation technology, such as generation and synthesis, personalised push, ranking, search filtering, and scheduling and decision-making, to provide internet information services in China. Providers must set up algorithm security management, regularly review their algorithms, models and data, label unmarked synthetic content, publicise how their services work, let users switch off recommendations or personal-feature targeting, and protect minors, the elderly, workers and consumers. Services with public-opinion attributes or social-mobilisation capacity must file their algorithms and undergo security assessments.
updates.notes: Adopted at the Cyberspace Administration of China's 20th office meeting of 2021 on 16 Nov 2021 with the consent of MIIT, the Ministry of Public Security and SAMR, signed on 31 Dec 2021, published on the CAC website on 4 Jan 2022 and in force from 1 Mar 2022 (Art. 35). The cyberspace authorities and the telecoms, public security and market regulation departments manage providers by class and grade according to public-opinion attributes, content, user numbers, data and the degree of intervention in user behaviour (Art. 23). Providers with public-opinion attributes or social-mobilisation capacity file through the internet information service algorithm filing system within ten working days of starting a service (Art. 24) and display their filing number (Art. 26). Breaches of the main duties can lead to warnings, suspension of information updates and fines of 10,000 to 100,000 yuan (Art. 31).

updates.summary: Trial measures that set up ethics review of science and technology activities involving human participants or laboratory animals, or posing ethics risks to life and health, the environment or public order. updates.notes: Issued by the Ministry of Science and Technology and nine other bodies with a notice of 7 Sept 2023, after approval by the Central Science and Technology Commission; published on the MOST website on 8 Oct 2023 and in force from 1 Dec 2023 (Art. 56). updates.summary: Decision of the NPC Standing Committee making 14 changes to the Cybersecurity Law. It adds an article on AI, Article 20 of the amended law: the state supports basic AI theory research and R&D of key technologies such as algorithms, builds training-data resources, computing power and other infrastructure, improves AI ethics norms, strengthens risk monitoring, assessment and safety supervision, and promotes AI applications and healthy development; it also supports using AI and other new technologies to improve cybersecurity protection. Other changes raise the penalties for network operators and critical information infrastructure operators.
updates.notes: Adopted on 28 Oct 2025 at the 18th session of the 14th NPC Standing Committee and in force from 1 Jan 2026. updates.summary: Framework law setting seven principles for government AI policy: sustainable development and well-being, human autonomy, privacy protection and data governance, cybersecurity and safety, transparency and explainability, fairness and non-discrimination, and accountability. The government must prevent AI uses that infringe life, body, liberty or property or involve discrimination or misleading information, and regulators must restrict or prohibit them. High-risk applications must carry warnings. MODA must promote an AI risk taxonomy and assessment framework and assessment tools, liability and remedies for high-risk AI must be defined, and agencies must risk-assess their own AI use.
updates.notes: Enacted in full (20 articles) by presidential order promulgated on 14 Jan 2026 (ROC 115-01-14), and in force from promulgation (Art. 20). Agencies must review the laws and administrative measures they administer and make, amend or repeal them within two years of the Act's effective date (Art. 18). The Executive Yuan must set up a National AI Strategic Committee, convened by the Premier with the NSTC handling its staff work, which formulates the National AI Development Guidelines and meets at least once a year (Art. 6). High-risk applications are those a central sector authority, in consultation with the Ministry of Digital Affairs, identifies as such (Art. 5(2)).

It lists 20 risk subtypes in three groups: technical design flaws, such as dangerous capabilities; post-deployment operation and human-AI interaction, such as deepfake fraud, cyberattacks and unauthorized actions by AI agents; and societal-structural and environmental impacts, such as cognitive warfare. Use cases that may seriously harm national security, fundamental rights, life and safety, property, social order or the environment are high-risk.

updates.summary: Draft recommended national standard, proposed by TC260, that sets out an AI security capability maturity model (ASMM) for assessing organisations, also usable by regulators as a reference. It covers data, model and application security in 15 security activities and 39 process areas, such as red-blue adversarial testing, value benchmark testing, backdoor detection, and security operations and emergency intervention. Each process area is assessed on the relevant ones of ten capabilities, among them robustness, explainability, fairness, rights protection and emerging-risk prevention, at five levels from informal execution to continuous optimisation, by self-assessment or a third party.
updates.notes: TC260 opened the draft for comment on 26 Aug 2026, with comments due by 25 Oct 2026. The draft has no standard number yet (GB/T XXXXX—XXXX) and leaves its publication and implementation dates blank. Organisations are typed as data-support, model-technology or application-service bodies, and each process area is mandatory, conditionally mandatory or optional for each type; an organisation reaches a level when all its applicable process areas reach it and no unaccepted major security risk remains. At the top level of post-training security, safeguards such as blocking knowledge of biological weapons and cyberattacks must not be removed or significantly weakened when the model runs in agents; at the top level of red-blue adversarial testing, organisations run human uplift trials that measure how far a model raises users' ability to write complex attack code or plan biological harm, and keep the uplift within safety thresholds. Normative references include GB/T 45654-2025 (CN-10), GB 45438-2025 (CN-08) and GB/T 45674-2025 (CN-24).
